name: Durendal
powers: Indestructible blade whose pommel holds relics of Saint Peter, Saint Basil and Saint Denis.
description: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland, is the greatest blade of the Frankish epic, carried by the hero and given to him, according to the poem, by the emperor Charlemagne. Its gilded pommel holds holy relics, a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil and hair of Saint Denis, making the sword a reliquary as much as a weapon. Wounded and dying after the rearguard's defeat at Roncevaux, Roland refuses to let the Saracens take the blade and tries to shatter it against a marble rock; the sword survives and the rock splits open. The same motif appears in the later Old French epic tradition, and a weapon reputed to be Durendal was long displayed at the church of Rocamadour in France. In Italian romance the blade passes to other heroes, including Ruggiero, showing how the object travelled across medieval literary cultures. Durendal stands beside Excalibur and Joyeuse as one of the archetypal Christian hero-swords of the Middle Ages.

name: Sword of Attila
material: Iron with gold and gem-set hilt
powers: Blade of world dominion pledged to Attila.
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun is known first from the Roman historian Jordanes, who writes in his Getica that a shepherd found a blade in the ground after cattle had trodden the place bare, and that Attila called it the Sword of Mars, a pledge of world dominion. By the eleventh century a richly decorated sabre was honoured in the Hungarian royal court as the Sword of Attila; the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld records that Queen Anastasia gave it to Otto, Duke of Bavaria, in 1063. The weapon that survives, kept in the imperial treasury of the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna and traditionally called the Sabre of Charlemagne, is in fact a Hungarian sabre of the early tenth century, long after Attila's death, with a gilded, gem-set hilt and curved blade of steppe form. The sword is sometimes said to have been recovered from Charlemagne's grave by Otto III in the year 1000, and to have been carried in the coronations of Holy Roman Emperors. No physical link to Attila can be proven, but the legend made the blade one of Europe's most famous royal relics.

name: Bogrács
description: The bogrács is the black cast-iron cauldron of Hungarian outdoor cooking, a three-legged pot suspended from a chain over an open fire, in which gulyás, pörkölt and fish stew are boiled and stirred with a long wooden spoon. The vessel dates from the world of the herdsmen of the Hungarian Plain, who cooked their one-pot meals over campfires, and the same pot is still the centrepiece of bográcsgulyás gatherings at weekends, feasts and village festivals. Its size and weight vary from small two-litre pots to great cauldrons for hundreds of eaters, and the cast iron is seasoned by use, giving the stew its characteristic smoky savour. Cooking in the bogrács is a slow, sociable ritual - the meat is seared, onion and paprika added, and the pot tended for hours - and for many Hungarians the cauldron over flame is the very image of hospitality and good eating.

name: Matyó Embroidery
description: Matyó embroidery is the flamboyant floral needlework of the Hungarian town of Mezőkövesd and its surrounding villages, where from about the 1860s women stitched huge roses, tulips and pansies in red, blue and green silk thread on white linen. The style covered festive women's costume, shirts, aprons, pillowcases, tablecloths and wall hangings, and the bold single blooms grew ever larger as the local Matyó identity took shape at the turn of the twentieth century. Unlike the fine satin stitch of other Hungarian regions, Matyó work used long, loose stitches that give the flowers a sculpted, three-dimensional look. The craft, passed from mother to daughter, was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2012, and embroiderers, fashion designers and textile artists in Mezőkövesd continue to develop it.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Hungarian textile studies

name: Székely Kapu
description: The Székely kapu is the carved wooden gateway of the Hungarian Székely villages of Transylvania, an oak structure built in two parts: a large wagon gate for carts and hay and a smaller door beside it for people on foot. The finest examples, carved from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, are covered with tulips, the tree of life, suns, rosettes and heraldic devices, and often bear inscriptions such as 'Isten hozott' ('God brought you') or the name and year of the householders. Folk belief held that the large gate belonged to the living and the small gate to the dead, who were carried through it one last time on their way to the grave. Because each gate recorded the family, the land and the faith of its owners, the surviving Székely gates - the earliest dated remnant is from Mikháza in 1673 - are read as genealogies in wood.
source: Hungarian and Székely ethnography of folk architecture

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the decorated shepherd's cloak of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length mantle of white felt cut from a single piece, split down the middle so the wearer can slip it over the shoulders and pin it under the chin. Its name pairs szűr, the plain cloak of Hungarian herdsmen, with cifra, 'ornamented', and indeed the best cifraszűr covers the felt with black, red and green wool applique arranged in rosettes, tulips, fringes and braided borders. Herdsmen wore the szűr against sun and rain and slept in it on the puszta, and a richly worked cloak was a sign of skill, wealth and pride, passed down in the family or given as a groom's gift. By the twentieth century the cifraszűr had moved from pasture to festival dress and museum collections, remaining a striking emblem of Hungarian shepherd culture.
material: white wool felt, coloured wool thread

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary, identified with the crown of the first king Saint Stephen I (ruled 1000-1038), is a circlet of gold hung with enamelled plaques, pearls and gemstones, with a distinctive cross set at an angle on top. Scholars date the surviving bands and figures to the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the crown as it exists today was almost certainly assembled from older parts for later coronations, so its precise age and original form are still debated. It was used to crown Hungarian kings from the Middle Ages down to Charles IV in 1916, the last Hungarian coronation, and legend held that no ruler who wore it could ever be overthrown. Hidden in chests, walled into castles and smuggled abroad over the centuries, the crown returned to Hungary from the United States in 1978 and has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building since 2000 as the supreme symbol of Hungarian statehood.
aliases: Crown of Saint Stephen of Hungary
source: Academic studies of the Hungarian coronation insignia
